beats.caption: Customer concentration: how much revenue a few buyers make up
beats.text: A supplier's revenue is the sum of what every customer buys. If thousands of customers each buy a little, losing one hardly matters. If a handful buy most of the output, the company's results depend on those few purchase decisions.

beats.caption: In AI hardware a few hyperscalers buy most of the output
beats.text: Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta and Oracle build most of the world's AI data centers, so chip, network and server suppliers sell a large share of their output to them. A supplier can have two or three customers making up half its revenue. Big orders arrive as large, lumpy purchase commitments.

beats.caption: Filers must disclose any customer at 10% or more
beats.text: US rules require a company to say when a single customer accounts for 10% or more of revenue, usually as 'Customer A, B, C' in the 10-K notes with the percentage. Risk factors often describe the largest buyers and what would happen if they cut back. Adding up these disclosures shows how concentrated a supplier is.

beats.caption: One buyer pulling back can move the whole company
beats.text: When a large customer pauses, switches to a rival, or designs its own chip in house, the supplier's revenue can fall by a double-digit percentage in a quarter. Fixed costs stay, so margins fall faster than revenue. Big buyers also use their weight to push prices down.

beats.caption: Concentration cuts both ways
beats.text: Selling to the biggest spenders means fast growth while their capex rises, and long design-in relationships are hard to displace. But the same few budgets drive the stock up and down, and in-house silicon programs are a standing threat. Related: NVIDIA (NVDA), Broadcom (AVGO), Marvell (MRVL), Super Micro Computer (SMCI).
